kpi: A packaging line is not a photograph on a supplier website. It is a set of machines, a set of people, and a set of order books that somebody else is competing for. Before you award a private label ribbon programme to any factory, you need evidence that the line as configured today can hold your standard six months from now - not a slide describing what the line could do if nobody else booked the same week.

faq: How long does a ribbon factory line review take, and who should attend?

Allow one full working day on site for a focused line review, and two days if you are evaluating a factory for the first time rather than for an additional programme. The strongest attendance is a team of three: a procurement or category manager who owns the commercial decision, a quality or technical engineer who can judge the process, and a person from your design or merchandising team who understands the product. A single buyer with no technical support tends to leave with good impressions and no usable evidence, because line capability questions cannot be answered by looking at finished goods alone.
What is the single most useful thing to check on a ribbon packaging line?

The changeover. Watch how the line moves from the previous customer's colour or construction to yours - how long it takes, who resets the machine, what is checked before the run starts, and how much of the set-up is recorded. Changeover time is the single best proxy for whether the factory is genuinely organised, because it exposes set-up discipline, tooling readiness, colour changeover practice and the presence of a real method at the same time. A factory with a tidy output but a forty-minute manual changeover is running on heroics, not on a system, and your programme will absorb that variability.
Should I require the factory to show me working samples rather than presentation swatches?

Yes, and you should insist that the samples are pulled from current production without being prepared for the meeting. Presentation swatches are selected, trimmed and often finished by hand, so they flatter the process. Ask for two or three rolls drawn from a running lot, ideally with the packing carton still closed so you can see how a real roll is wound, labelled and packed. Handle them yourself: a ribbon that feels stiff, slides badly or has a slightly ragged selvedge in the hand tells you more about the line than a signed capability statement does.
How do I verify capacity claims that are based on machine count rather than actual output?

Machine count tells you the theoretical ceiling, not the achievable output, and the gap between them is where your delivery dates get missed. Ask the factory to show you the actual loading log or production record for the previous four to eight weeks and compare it with the number of machines running. Then ask what happens to the queue when a machine goes down for a day. A plant with twenty looms running fifteen looms is not a twenty-loom plant, and a plant that will not show you loading records has not earned the right to quote you a lead time you can plan against.
What should I do if the factory looks excellent but the paperwork is thin?

Separate the two findings rather than averaging them into a single verdict. A strong physical operation with incomplete quality records often means records are being written after the fact, which is a fixable process problem but one that must be fixed before volume. Ask specifically for the last three incoming inspection reports, two pre-shipment inspection reports and one corrective action record, and ask to see the originals with dates. If they can produce those, the evidence gap is a paperwork problem you can schedule. If they cannot, you are looking at an unstructured operation, and no amount of good behaviour on the day of your visit will change that.
Do I need to do a line review before every new programme?

No. Do a full review when you are selecting a new supplier, when you are adding a new factory to a qualified list, or when something has gone wrong badly enough that you need to understand why. For an existing factory adding a second programme, a shorter and more targeted review usually serves you better: confirm that the specific line and the specific decoration method you need are available, check the last three production records for that construction, and review the two most recent pre-shipment inspection reports for that product. Repeating a full audit for every new style burns goodwill and rarely changes the decision.
